messages.subject: spatialFastMaps bug?
messages.subject_clean: spatialFastMaps bug?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

When running spatialFastMaps in Cardinal 2.4.0, there seems to be a possible bug (unless this was intentional) in the functions .spatialFastmap2 and .findDistantObjects2 when iterating over FastMap components. It appears that xa and xb (spatial neighbors?), which should be matrices, are typed as numeric if there is only one column. It seems that adding these lines of code (highlighted in red) seems to fix the issue, though I am curious if this behavior is intentional.

.spatialFastmap2 <- function(x, r, ncomp, method, metric, dist,
                            tol.dist, iter.max = 2, BPPARAM)
{
    init <- TRUE
    wts <- spatialWeights(x, r=r, method=method,
                        dist=dist, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
    spatial <- list(r=r, weights=c(wts),
        neighbors=attr(wts, "neighbors"),
        offsets=attr(wts, "offsets"))
    proj <- matrix(0, nrow=ncol(x), ncol=ncomp)
    pivots <- matrix(NA_integer_, nrow=ncomp, ncol=2)
    # suppress progress in inner parallel loop
    progress <- getOption("Cardinal.progress")
    options(Cardinal.progress=FALSE)
    on.exit(options(Cardinal.progress=progress))
    # spatially-aware distance functions
    fun <- function(xbl, xa, xb) {
        i <- attr(attr(xbl, "idx"), "centers")
        d_ai <- .spatialDistance2(xbl, xa,
            offsets=attr(xbl, "offsets"),
            weights=attr(xbl, "params"),
            ref.offsets=attr(xa, "offsets"),
            ref.weights=attr(xa, "weights"),
            neighbors=attr(xbl, "neighbors"),
            metric=metric, i=i, j=attr(xa, "idx"),
            proj=proj, tol.dist=tol.dist)
        d_bi <- .spatialDistance2(xbl, xb,
            offsets=attr(xbl, "offsets"),
            weights=attr(xbl, "params"),
            ref.offsets=attr(xb, "offsets"),
            ref.weights=attr(xb, "weights"),
            neighbors=attr(xbl, "neighbors"),
            metric=metric, i=i, j=attr(xb, "idx"),
            proj=proj, tol.dist=tol.dist)
        (d_ai^2 + d_ab^2 - d_bi^2) / (2 * d_ab)
    }
    # iterate over FastMap components
    for ( j in seq_len(ncomp) ) {
        o_ab <- .findDistantObjects2(x, proj=proj, spatial=spatial,
            metric=metric, dist=dist, tol.dist=tol.dist,
            init=init, iter.max=iter.max, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
        if ( any(is.na <http://is.na>(o_ab)) )
            break
        if ( !is.null(attr(o_ab, "init")) )
            init <- attr(o_ab, "init")
        pivots[j,] <- o_ab
        oa <- pivots[j,1]
        ob <- pivots[j,2]
        xa <- iData(x)[,spatial$neighbors[[oa]]]
        if (class(xa) == 'numeric') {
            xa <- as.matrix(xa)
        }
        attr(xa, "idx") <- oa
        attr(xa, "offsets") <- spatial$offsets[[oa]]
        attr(xa, "weights") <- spatial$weights[[oa]]
        xb <- iData(x)[,spatial$neighbors[[ob]]]
        if (class(xb) == 'numeric') {
            xb <- as.matrix(xb)
        }
        attr(xb, "idx") <- ob
        attr(xb, "offsets") <- spatial$offsets[[ob]]
        attr(xb, "weights") <- spatial$weights[[ob]]
        d_ab <- .spatialDistance2(xa, xb,
            offsets=list(spatial$offsets[[oa]]),
            weights=list(spatial$weights[[oa]]),
            ref.offsets=spatial$offsets[[ob]],
            ref.weights=spatial$weights[[ob]],
            neighbors=list(seq_len(ncol(xa))),
            metric=metric, i=oa, j=ob,
            proj=proj, tol.dist=tol.dist)
        comp_j <- spatialApply(x, .r=spatial$r, .fun=fun, xa=xa, xb=xb,
            .blocks=TRUE, .simplify=.unlist_and_reorder, .dist=dist,
            .init=init, .params=spatial$weights, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
        .message(".", appendLF=FALSE)
        proj[,j] <- comp_j
    }
    .message(" ")
    do_rbind <- function(ans) do.call("rbind", ans)
    corr <- featureApply(x, function(xbl) {
        t(apply(xbl, 1, function(xi) {
            vapply(1:ncomp, function(j) {
                comp_j <- proj[,j]
                if ( all(comp_j == 0) ) {
                    0
                } else {
                    cor(xi, comp_j)
                }
            }, numeric(1))
        }))
    }, .blocks=TRUE, .simplify=do_rbind, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
    colnames(proj) <- paste("FC", 1:ncomp, sep="")
    colnames(corr) <- paste("FC", 1:ncomp, sep="")
    pivots <- as.data.frame(pivots)
    names(pivots) <- c("Oa", "Ob")
    sdev <- apply(proj, 2, sd)
    list(scores=proj, correlation=corr, pivots=pivots, sdev=sdev)
}

.findDistantObjects2 <- function(x, proj, spatial, metric, dist,
                            tol.dist, init, iter.max, BPPARAM)
{
    iter <- 1
    oa <- 1
    ob <- NULL
    fun <- function(xbl, xj) {
        i <- attr(attr(xbl, "idx"), "centers")
        .spatialDistance2(xbl, xj,
            offsets=attr(xbl, "offsets"),
            weights=attr(xbl, "params"),
            ref.offsets=attr(xj, "offsets"),
            ref.weights=attr(xj, "weights"),
            neighbors=attr(xbl, "neighbors"),
            metric=metric, i=i, j=attr(xj, "idx"),
            proj=proj, tol.dist=tol.dist)
    }
    while ( iter <= iter.max ) {
        xa <- iData(x)[,spatial$neighbors[[oa]]]
        if (class(xa) == 'numeric') {
            xa <- as.matrix(xa)
        }
        attr(xa, "idx") <- oa
        attr(xa, "offsets") <- spatial$offsets[[oa]]
        attr(xa, "weights") <- spatial$weights[[oa]]
        dists <- spatialApply(x, .r=spatial$r, .fun=fun, xj=xa,
            .blocks=TRUE, .simplify=.unlist_and_reorder, .dist=dist,
            .init=init, .params=spatial$weights, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
        if ( !is.null(attr(dists, "init")) )
            init <- attr(dists, "init")
        cand <- which.max(dists)
        if ( dists[cand] == 0 )
            return(structure(c(NA, NA), init=init))
        if ( isTRUE(ob == cand) )
            return(structure(c(oa, ob), init=init))
        ob <- cand
        xb <- iData(x)[,spatial$neighbors[[ob]]]
        if (class(xb) == 'numeric') {
            xb <- as.matrix(xb)
        }
        attr(xb, "idx") <- ob
        attr(xb, "offsets") <- spatial$offsets[[ob]]
        attr(xb, "weights") <- spatial$weights[[ob]]
        dists <- spatialApply(x, .r=spatial$r, .fun=fun, xj=xb,
            .blocks=TRUE, .simplify=.unlist_and_reorder, .dist=dist,
            .init=init, .params=spatial$weights, BPPARAM=BPPARAM)
        oa <- which.max(dists)
        d <- dists[oa]
        if ( dists[oa] == 0 )
            return(structure(c(NA, NA), init=init))
        iter <- iter + 1
    }
    structure(c(oa, ob), init=init)
}

They may be unrelated issues.

The warning shouldn't impact any pre-processing methods, as they don't rely on the spatial information. It is just letting you know that spectra with duplicate spatial coordinates exist in the dataset. This may cause issues with spatial methods, but shouldn't result in errors. This usually happens when the original spatial coordinates are in real-world units; converting to imzML requires the x/y-coordinates be on a regular pixel grid, which isn't always possible to do perfectly. The original coordinates are sometimes preserved in the pixelData() if they were included in the imzML using known userParam tags.

I'm not sure about the source of the pre-processing error without more information.

-Kylie

SNR really isn't a great for this, because it depends greatly on how the noise is calculated, which can vary by definition and algorithm, and Cardinal's pre-processing also throws it away immediately because keeping it for every peak would double the size of the output dataset.

Assuming you have multiple tissues from each prep condition, the most straightforward thing to do with your current data would be to use meansTest() or segmentationTest(). They are designed exactly for statistically testing significant differences in abundance between conditions.

Ultimately, it sounds like what you actually want may be to do a Limit-of-Detection experiment, where you spike in a solution at known concentrations and calculate a calibration curve for sample prep (e.g., something like https://onlinelibrary-wiley-com.ezproxy.neu.edu/doi/pdfdirect/10.1002/pmic.201500515).

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
While not necessarily unexpected behavior, the example shown does seem weird.

The tolerance is used when matching the detected peaks to a reference m/z list, but it is not used to create that reference (e.g., from the mean spectrum) if none is provided.

However, the mean spectrum calculation will now happen on the centroided representation. Ideally this improves sensitivity of low-intensity peaks, but it could result in duplicate peaks like this if there is enough error in the peak's m/z values to result in large gaps in the detected peaks' centroids between different spectra.

To fix this, you can do peak picking on the mean spectrum calculated from the full profile spectra first, and then provide the output of this as the reference.

The CardinalWorfklows "Segmentation" vignette shows an example of this: http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/vignettes/CardinalWorkflows/inst/doc/MSI-segmentation.html

That being said, I'm curious what's going on here. If the data is reasonable size, can you send it to me?

Thanks,
Kylie

1. The normalization may be affecting the image, depending on the distribution of the rest of the ions in the spectra.

If the data is small enough that the normalized profile spectra can fit in memory, you could try checking the image after normalization only.

2. At 1034.56, a tolerance of 10 ppm is roughly 0.01 m/z, which is wider than the 0.001 m/z specified in the image.

Doing peakAlign() performs an implicit binning of any peaks detected within that tolerance, so it may be capturing a nearby adjacent peak for the lower row but not the top row.

3. Likely related to either (1) or (2) above, notice that the intensity scale is much different after the processing.

The ion intensities in the first row may still be detected, but much lower after some combination of the possible issues caused by (1) and (2).

I would check the image trying different combinations of no normalization and/or adjusting the tolerance to peakAlign(). I would also try widening the 'plusminus' in the original image and seeing if that leads to an image similar to the post-processing image.

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
In most cases, the sample size in MSI isn't going to be large enough to be able to specify "random", so you usually only need to specify "fixed" and "groups".

Then "fixed" is just a one-sided formula specifying the condition, which should be a column in pixelData. Cardinal will add the left-hand side the formula itself after summarizing over the groups (samples).

And "groups" is actually the sample identifier: all spectra in the same group will be summarized together before testing. Specifying this correctly depends on how your samples were laid out when gathering the data. If you just had one-tissue-sample-per-slide/run, then you can just use run(). If you had multiple-tissue-samples-per-slide/run, then you'll need to create a new pixelData column identifying each unique tissue sample in the dataset. In the RCC example dataset from CardinalWorkflows, each slide has two tissues, so this can be done by combining run() and $diagnosis: http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/vignettes/CardinalWorkflows/inst/doc/MSI-testing.html

You can only really specify "random" if you have enough multiple samples per condition per slide, in which case you can control for variation between runs by specifying it as a random effect. It can help to control against the strong chance that you detecting random variation between runs rather than an actual difference between conditions.

For you, the syntax will probably look something like:

fit <- meansTest(mse, ~ prep_type, groups = run(mse))

or

fit <- meansTest(mse, ~ prep_type, groups = mse$my_samples)

depending on whether you need to create a new column to uniquely indicate the tissue samples.

-Kylie
